overview: The Republic of Turkey was proclaimed on 29 October 1923 after the Ottoman Empire’s collapse. This atlas label starts in 1930, so it misses the republic’s founding years. It follows the modern state through changes in government, institutions and everyday life; it is not a claim that all earlier societies of Anatolia were one Turkish civilization.

periods.title: Republican reforms and postwar change
periods.summary: The map begins after the republic’s establishment. Secular reforms and constitutional changes preceded a postwar era of competing political parties.

periods.title: Military intervention and constitutional politics
periods.summary: A military takeover in 1960 was followed by the 1961 constitution; a 1971 military memorandum brought further restrictions and amendments.

periods.title: Coup and a new constitutional framework
periods.summary: The 1980 coup suspended the constitution and dissolved political parties. The 1982 constitution subsequently underwent many amendments.

periods.title: Political consolidation and a failed coup
periods.summary: Recep Tayyip Erdoğan became prime minister in 2003. A failed coup in 2016 was followed by extensive repression and institutional changes.

periods.title: Executive presidency
periods.summary: The presidential system took effect in 2018. Dated reporting through September 2025 describes continuing political competition and serious civil-liberties concerns.

items.text: Ankara became the republic’s capital, while Istanbul remained a major city. The early atlas shapes are incomplete: the 1930 and 1938 mainland features stop near 39.35 degrees east, omitting much of eastern Turkey. The larger outline appearing in 1945 must not be mistaken for evidence of a vast new conquest.

Women gained the right to vote and stand for national election through a constitutional amendment on 5 December 1934. The same decade saw secularism explicitly added to the constitution. Legal changes reshaped citizenship, although a right written into law did not automatically remove every obstacle in daily life.

Turkey joined NATO in 1952, becoming part of the Cold War’s Western alliance system. Its position beside the Black Sea and the straits made it strategically important. Alliance membership did not remove disagreements: relations with fellow member Greece were repeatedly strained over Cyprus and other regional questions.

Army interventions repeatedly interrupted parliamentary government. The 1960 takeover brought arrests of the country’s political leadership; after the 1980 coup, political parties were dissolved. Constitutions are therefore part of a struggle over authority, not proof that elections and freedoms operated continuously.

The failed coup of 2016 killed hundreds. The government’s response included mass detention and the closure or takeover of schools, businesses and media outlets. These events affected much more than officeholders: families could lose work, educational institutions or trusted sources of news.

A constitutional referendum in 2017 and elections in 2018 completed the move from a prime-minister-led government to an executive presidency. September 2025 congressional research also records concerns about restrictions on expression and the fairness of political competition. This is a dated assessment, not an assumption that every citizen supported the same policies.

Making flatbread can be a family team project. UNESCO’s 2016 multinational description includes people dividing preparation and baking tasks, with neighbours joining in rural communities. It specifically records a Turkish wedding custom of giving bread to the couple’s neighbours. A meal could help introduce a new household to the people next door.

Turkish coffee names a preparation tradition, not beans grown only in Turkey. Finely ground coffee is prepared in a long-handled pot called a cezve and served in small cups, often with water and a sweet. A 2023 UNESCO account describes coffee as an invitation to sit, talk and spend time together.

That UNESCO account also describes some engagement visits where a prospective bride serves the groom salty coffee. His willingness to drink it becomes part of the teasing ritual. It is a custom practised by some families, not a national requirement: the coffee can arrive with a little more drama than expected.

Ebru artists make patterns float before they put them on paper. They sprinkle or brush pigments onto a prepared liquid, shape flowers or swirling designs, and transfer the surface pattern to a sheet. Marbled paper has decorated bookbindings. The result can look like a tiny weather system persuaded to sit still.

Learning ebru traditionally involves watching a skilled practitioner and practising together, rather than simply following a printed recipe. UNESCO’s 2014 description emphasizes oral teaching and master-apprentice relationships. Workshops can also be social places where conversation accompanies careful handwork.

The Health Transformation Plan began in 2003. WHO’s 2018 assessment describes family health centres and community health centres intended to make everyday care easier to reach. Insurance expanded and patients’ direct payments fell, but workforce needs and long-term illnesses still posed challenges. Improving access involved organization and staffing as well as hospital buildings.

After the February 2023 earthquakes, safe water became part of rebuilding ordinary routines. UNICEF’s July account describes repairs, water-quality tests, storage and deliveries by truck to temporary settlements. Cooking dinner, washing clothes and caring for a baby all depended on restoring services that are easy to overlook when the tap works.

The same response installed toilets and showers and supplied family hygiene kits with soap, towels and sanitary products. Municipal partners also worked on waste management. A functioning toilet was not a decorative finishing touch to recovery: it protected privacy, dignity and the ability to live together in crowded temporary accommodation.

In Hatay, parent educators held sessions beside tents, in courtyards and in the shade of temporary containers. UNICEF’s December 2023 report describes bilingual staff working with Turkish citizens and Syrian refugees. Parents could ask about feeding and early development close to where they were living, even without a normal classroom.

One participant, Meryem, attended with her two-year-old son Özgür and examined nutrition leaflets. Other parents learned of sessions through neighbours. These are glimpses of families exchanging information and trying to care for children after a disaster, rather than a single model of how all Turkish households raise children.

Nine-year-old Meryem in Osmaniye had lost access to her damaged home and school after the earthquakes. In a May 2023 report she was practising multiplication at a child-friendly centre while her family lived in a container. Lessons, games and a welcoming teacher helped restore parts of her daily routine.

This Meryem wanted to become a teacher and already enjoyed explaining things to her siblings. She also played catch with new friends, while still missing her old school. Rebuilding childhood meant more than replacing a desk: friendship, play and familiar routines mattered too.

A 2024 education needs survey asked 4,156 households from different national backgrounds about barriers to learning. Respondents identified problems including nutritious food, clean drinking water and toilets. These practical needs belonged in an education discussion alongside attendance and access for children with disabilities; the survey was not a census of every school.

Aziz Sancar grew up in Savur in southeastern Turkey. His parents had not received formal education but valued their children’s schooling. He studied in Istanbul and later in the United States. His path shows how family encouragement and opportunities across national borders could connect a small town with international scientific research.

In 1983 Sancar’s studies of bacteria explained how repair enzymes deal with DNA damaged by ultraviolet light. He shared the 2015 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for research on DNA repair. Cells, it turns out, have repair work to do too. This was international laboratory science, not a claim that one country alone made the discovery.

Modern archaeology in Turkey also changed knowledge of much earlier societies. Excavation at Göbekli Tepe began in 1995 through the Şanlıurfa Museum and German Archaeological Institute. The project’s own history credits local families who reported finds and a farmer who guided an archaeologist to the mound. Discovery depended on people who knew the fields.

That project brings together specialists in animal remains, stone tools, buildings, geography and microscopic plant evidence. Their work concerns prehistoric communities thousands of years before the republic. A modern state can support research into an ancient past without claiming that it built every monument inside today’s borders.

The alphabet reform of 1928, just before this map record begins, replaced the Arabic-based Ottoman Turkish writing system with Latin-based Turkish letters. The law required the new letters in schools and official business, with a transition timetable. Reading a newspaper or completing a form became part of a major change in public life.

A short Turkish sample is “Egemenlik, kayıtsız şartsız Milletindir.” Article 6 of the 1982 Constitution, as reproduced by the Constitutional Court in its amended text, means “Sovereignty belongs to the Nation without any restriction or condition.” Turkish here already uses a Latin-based alphabet; this is the actual written wording, not a transliteration from an older script.

ending.text: The republic continues; coups, constitutional amendments and the shift to a presidency changed its institutions without ending the country. Its recent history includes strong political disagreements and restrictions on rights. The political account here is dated through September 2025, while individual family and recovery stories retain their own reporting dates.
